newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rhone-Poulenc could have gene Parkinson treatment.
newsitem.headline: Rhone-Poulenc could have gene Parkinson treatment.

text.p: Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc, the drugs company majority-owned by France's Rhone-Poulenc SA, said on Tuesday it may be on the road to a successful gene therapy in the fight against Parkinson's disease.

A study published in Tuesday's Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences medical journal shows that a new gene therapy significantly improved survival of key neurones in an animal model of the debilitating disease.
Parkinson's disease affects about two out of every 1,000 people after the age of 50, and is one of the most common neurologic disorders of the elderly.

Researchers from RPR's Gencell unit and the French state-research institute Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS) demonstrated in their article that a technique called recombinant adenovirus encoding glial-cell-line derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) significantly protected neurones from degenerating.
It also prevented behavioural deficits in a rat model of Parkinson's disease.
"These results suggest that gene therapy is of therapeutic value for Parkinson's disease," said Frederic Revah, co-author of the study and head of Central Nervous System R&D at RPR Gencell.
"This finding further supports the potential to lead to the development for Parkinson's disease based on the use of recombinant adenoviral vectors encoding neurothropic factors," he said.

GDNF is a neuroprotective agent which was shown to protect those dopaminergic neurones which are specifically affected in Parkinson's disease. But GDNF does not normally cross the blood-brain barrier.
Gene transfer will enable GDNF to be expressed inside the brain, circumventing the barrier, and making the neuroprotection effective.
Scientists from RPR and CNRS constructed a vector allowing the transfer of the gene-encoding GDNF to reach the brain via a genetically modified adenovirus.
They injected this vector into the region of the rat brain corresponding to the region normally affected in Parkinson's patients.

This gene therapy was found to protect dopaminergic neurones from the effects of a toxin that normally causes cell death and prevented the motor deficits that result from dopaminergic neurone degeneration.
Dopamine is one of the substances used by neurones to transmit impulses and is normally produced in a part of the brain that participates in the control of movement -- the basal ganglia.
In Parkinson's disease patients, deterioration of this area of the brain reduces the amount of dopamine and other transmitters such as acetycholine.
Without dopamine, the nerve cells cannot properly transmit messages and this results in impairment of motor functions.
RPR said that the exact reasons why the cells of the brains deteriorate is still unknown.
